solution:
Living organisms are classified because it is **nearly impossible to study all the living organisms** one by one; classification makes their study possible.

1. The number of known and described species is very large (about **1.7-1.8 million**), and new organisms are continuously being identified.
2. **Classification** groups organisms into **convenient categories (taxa)** based on easily observable characters, so the moment a group is named (plants, mammals, dogs), the characters of its members are known.
3. It helps in **identification** of an organism and in giving it a correct **scientific name** (nomenclature).
4. It brings out the **similarities and dissimilarities** among organisms and the **relationships** among them, including evolutionary relationships (systematics).
5. It places each organism in a **hierarchy of categories** (species, genus, family, order, class, phylum or division, kingdom), which makes the study of the diversity of life orderly.
groundedIn: §1.1; §1.2 — 1.7-1.8 million species known; nearly impossible to study all living organisms, so classification into convenient categories based on easily observable characters; taxa; systematics and evolutionary relationships; knowledge of characters identifies similarities and dissimilarities

stem: Why are the classification systems changing every now and then?
solution:
Classification systems keep changing because our **knowledge of organisms keeps growing**, and classification is revised to match it.

1. As we explore new areas, and even old ones, **new organisms are continuously being identified**, and a large number still remain unknown. Each new organism has to be placed in the system.
2. The basis of classification has widened. The earliest classifications were based on the **uses** of organisms; modern taxonomy uses **external and internal structure, structure of the cell, development process and ecological information**.
3. **Systematics** now takes into account the **evolutionary relationships** between organisms, so groups are rearranged as these relationships become clearer.
4. Taxonomists have developed **sub-categories** in the hierarchy to allow a more sound and scientific placement of taxa.
groundedIn: §1.1; §1.2.7 — new organisms continuously being identified; earliest classifications based on uses; modern taxonomy uses external and internal structure, cell structure, development process and ecological information; systematics takes into account evolutionary relationships; sub-categories developed for more sound and scientific placement

stem: What different criteria would you choose to classify people that you meet often?
solution:
People met often can be grouped into **convenient categories based on easily observable characters**, as in any classification. Possible criteria:

1. **Sex**: male and female.
2. **Age**: children, adults, elderly people.
3. **Height or build**: tall, medium, short.
4. **Language spoken** or the **region** they come from.
5. **Occupation**: students, teachers, doctors, shopkeepers and so on.
6. **Relationship** to oneself: family members, relatives, friends, neighbours.

As in taxonomy, these can be arranged in levels (for example, people → students → students of one class), each lower group sharing more characters.
groundedIn: §1.1; §1.2.7 — classification groups anything into convenient categories based on some easily observable characters; lower the taxa, more are the characteristics that the members share

stem: What do we learn from identification of individuals and populations?
solution:
Identification tells us **exactly which organism** we are dealing with, so that it can be named, classified and related to other organisms.

1. **Correct naming:** nomenclature is only possible when the organism is described correctly and we know to what organism the name is attached. Identification makes it possible to give it its **scientific name**, the same all over the world.
2. **Characters:** we learn the characters of an individual or group, which brings out the **similarities and dissimilarities** among individuals of the same kind and of other kinds.
3. **Place in classification:** knowing the characters, the organism can be placed in the right **taxonomic categories** (species, genus, family and so on).
4. **Relationships:** it shows how organisms are related to each other, which is the subject of **systematics**.
5. **Diversity:** identifying the different kinds (species) of organisms in an area tells us about its **biodiversity**, and new organisms continue to be identified.
groundedIn: §1.1; §1.2 — nomenclature only possible when the organism is described correctly (identification); each different kind represents a species, biodiversity; systematics studies relationships; knowledge of characters helps identify similarities and dissimilarities and place an organism in categories

stem:
Given below is the scientific name of Mango. Identify the correctly written name.

Mangifera Indica

Mangifera indica
solution:
**Mangifera indica** is the correctly written name.

1. In a biological name the first word, denoting the **genus** (Mangifera), starts with a **capital letter**, while the **specific epithet** (indica) starts with a **small letter**.
2. In Mangifera Indica the specific epithet wrongly begins with a capital letter.
3. The name is printed in italics, or, when handwritten, both words are separately underlined.
groundedIn: §1.1 — the first word denoting the genus starts with a capital letter while the specific epithet starts with a small letter, illustrated with Mangifera indica; printed in italics or separately underlined when handwritten

stem: Define a taxon. Give some examples of taxa at different hierarchical levels.
solution:
A **taxon** (plural **taxa**) is a unit of classification: each taxonomic category, which represents a **rank** in the taxonomic hierarchy.

**Examples:** plants, animals, mammals, dogs, wheat and rice are all taxa, but at different levels. A dog is a mammal and mammals are animals, so dogs, mammals and animals are taxa at different levels.

Taxa at different hierarchical levels for man:

| Level | Taxon |
|---|---|
| Kingdom | Animalia |
| Phylum | Chordata |
| Class | Mammalia |
| Order | Primata |
| Family | Hominidae |
| Genus | Homo |
| Species | sapiens (Homo sapiens) |
groundedIn: §1.1; §1.2; §1.2.7; Table 1.1 — taxa are convenient categories at very different levels (plants, wheat, animals, mammals, dogs); each category represents a rank and is termed taxon (pl. taxa); Kingdom Animalia; man in Table 1.1: Homo, Hominidae, Primata, Mammalia, Chordata

stem:
Can you identify the correct sequence of taxonomical categories?

(a) Species → Order → Phylum → Kingdom

(b) Genus → Species → Order → Kingdom

(c) Species → Genus → Order → Phylum
solution:
**(a) and (c)** are both correct sequences; **(b)** is incorrect.

1. In ascending order the categories are **species → genus → family → order → class → phylum → kingdom**, species being the lowest category.
2. (a) and (c) each leave out some categories, but the ones they list follow this ascending order.
3. (b) is wrong because **genus** is a higher category than **species** (a genus is an aggregate of closely related species), so it cannot come before species.
groundedIn: §1.2; §1.2.2; Fig. 1.1 — common categories kingdom, phylum or division, class, order, family, genus and species, species the lowest category; genera are aggregates of closely related species; categories in ascending order starting with species

context: Define and understand the following terms:
solution:
**Phylum** is the taxonomic category above class: it comprises related **classes** that share a few common features.

Example: classes comprising fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals are placed in phylum **Chordata**, based on common features like the presence of **notochord** and **dorsal hollow neural system**. In plants, the corresponding category is called **Division**.
groundedIn: §1.2.6 — classes comprising fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds along with mammals constitute phylum; Chordata based on notochord and dorsal hollow neural system; in plants the category is called Division

context: Define and understand the following terms:
solution:
**Class** is the taxonomic category that includes related **orders**.

Example: order **Primata** (monkey, gorilla, gibbon) and order **Carnivora** (tiger, cat, dog) are placed in class **Mammalia**, which has other orders also.
groundedIn: §1.2.5 — class includes related orders; order Primata placed in class Mammalia along with order Carnivora

context: Define and understand the following terms:
solution:
**Family** is the taxonomic category made of a group of related **genera**, with still fewer similarities than genus and species. In plants, families are characterised on the basis of both **vegetative and reproductive features**.

Examples: the genera Solanum, Petunia and Datura are placed in family **Solanaceae**; the genera Panthera (lion, tiger, leopard) and Felis (cats) are placed in family **Felidae**.
groundedIn: §1.2.3 — family has a group of related genera with still less number of similarities; characterised on vegetative and reproductive features; Solanum, Petunia and Datura in Solanaceae; Panthera and Felis in Felidae

context: Define and understand the following terms:
solution:
**Order** is a higher taxonomic category: an assemblage of **families** which exhibit a few similar characters. Order and other higher categories are identified on the basis of **aggregates of characters**.

Examples: plant families Convolvulaceae and Solanaceae are included in the order **Polymoniales**, mainly on floral characters (the book's spelling; the order is usually written Polemoniales). The animal order **Carnivora** includes the families Felidae and Canidae.
groundedIn: §1.2.4 — order is the assemblage of families which exhibit a few similar characters; higher categories identified on aggregates of characters; Convolvulaceae and Solanaceae in Polymoniales on floral characters; Carnivora includes Felidae and Canidae

context: Define and understand the following terms:
solution:
**Genus** is a group of related **species** which has more characters in common in comparison to species of other genera; genera are aggregates of closely related species.

Examples: potato and brinjal are different species of the genus **Solanum**; lion (Panthera leo), leopard (P. pardus) and tiger (P. tigris) are species of the genus **Panthera**, which differs from the genus Felis (cats).
groundedIn: §1.2.2 — genus comprises a group of related species with more characters in common; potato and brinjal in Solanum; lion, leopard and tiger in Panthera, which differs from Felis

stem: Illustrate the taxonomical hierarchy with suitable examples of a plant and an animal.
solution:
The **taxonomic hierarchy** is the arrangement of taxonomic categories in a sequence of ranks, from **species** (lowest) to **kingdom** (highest). As we go higher, the number of common characteristics among members goes on decreasing.

| Category | Plant: Mango | Animal: Man |
|---|---|---|
| Kingdom | Plantae | Animalia |
| Division / Phylum | Angiospermae | Chordata |
| Class | Dicotyledonae | Mammalia |
| Order | Sapindales | Primata |
| Family | Anacardiaceae | Hominidae |
| Genus | Mangifera | Homo |
| Species | indica (Mangifera indica) | sapiens (Homo sapiens) |

The same hierarchy holds for wheat (Triticum aestivum: Triticum, Poaceae, Poales, Monocotyledonae, Angiospermae) and for housefly (Musca domestica: Musca, Muscidae, Diptera, Insecta, Arthropoda).
groundedIn: §1.2; §1.2.7; Fig. 1.1; Table 1.1 — all categories together constitute the taxonomic hierarchy; Kingdom Animalia and Kingdom Plantae; categories from species to kingdom in ascending order; as we go higher the common characteristics decrease; man, housefly, mango and wheat with their categories
